name: KPV
lead: KPV is a tripeptide made of lysine, proline and valine (Lys-Pro-Val). It corresponds to the C-terminal end (residues 11 to 13) of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH), a peptide that regulates pigmentation and also influences inflammation [1][4]. KPV is the portion of the hormone that retains anti-inflammatory activity but lacks the sequence motif associated with pigment and other melanocortin-receptor effects [4][6].

In peptide and recovery communities KPV is discussed as an 'inflammation' peptide, for gut inflammation, skin irritation and general recovery, and it is often mentioned as one component of a bundle with BPC-157, TB-500 and GHK-Cu. The research behind it consists mainly of cell and rodent studies, particularly mouse colitis models. No published human clinical trial of KPV for appearance, recovery or inflammatory disease was identified in the sources reviewed [2][5].

KPV is not an approved drug. It is sold as a research peptide, and a 2026 review of peptide use in sport and bodybuilding groups it with other peptides marketed for recovery and anti-inflammatory effects while stating that clinical evidence supporting such use is limited [2].

paras: Alpha-MSH is a 13-amino-acid hormone derived from proopiomelanocortin that has potent anti-inflammatory and protective effects in many animal models, but its pigmentary effects have limited its development as a medicine for inflammatory disorders [6]. Researchers found that short fragments of the molecule retain much of the anti-inflammatory activity. A 2010 review notes that KPV, the C-terminal tripeptide, lacks the sequence motif required for melanocortin-receptor-mediated pigmentation, which is why it attracted interest as an alternative [4].

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source that may contain errors, describes KPV as synthesised by standard solid-phase peptide synthesis, as having a molecular weight of about 342 Da, and as unstable in acidic and alkaline conditions, degrading mainly to a cyclic diketopiperazine, which it says drives the use of protective formulations in studies of oral delivery [7].

KPV has no approved medical use. In community discussion it is taken or injected for gut inflammation, for tendon and soft-tissue recovery as part of peptide 'stacks', and sometimes for skin conditions [13][14]. Forum users describe a four-peptide bundle sometimes called 'KLOW' (KPV, BPC-157, TB-500 and GHK-Cu), describing the first three as being for soft tissue and inflammation and the copper peptide for skin and hair [13][14].

Alpha-MSH and its fragments, including KPV, reduce production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, and a key step is inhibition of the transcription factor NF-kappa B [1][3]. Reviews note that alpha-MSH acts through melanocortin receptors on immune and peripheral cells and through descending neural pathways, and that KPV can act on inflammatory cells directly [1][6].

In cell and mouse work, KPV was reported to enter inflamed intestinal epithelial cells through the peptide transporter PepT1 and reduce intestinal inflammation [8]. Grokipedia states that KPV acts in part independently of classical melanocortin receptors [7]. Early antimicrobial studies found that alpha-MSH and KPV inhibited growth of Staphylococcus aureus and Candida albicans in laboratory tests [9][3].

Because small peptides are broken down in the gut, much of the animal research has used engineered delivery systems. Examples include polymer nanoparticles loaded with KPV that targeted the colon in mice [10], hyaluronic acid-functionalised nanoparticles given orally in a mouse model of ulcerative colitis [11], and a KPV-binding hydrogel studied for restoring the mucosal barrier in an inflamed colon [12]. These are experimental formulations rather than the unformulated powders sold by vendors.

A 2008 study reported anti-inflammatory potential of KPV in murine models of inflammatory bowel disease [15]. A broader review of alpha-MSH-related tripeptides concluded that these peptides showed protective and anti-inflammatory effects in vitro and in vivo in models including contact dermatitis, vasculitis, fibrosis, arthritis and gastrointestinal inflammation, and discussed future treatment of immune-mediated disease [6]. A 2025 review of host-defence peptides for inflammatory bowel disease lists KPV among candidates, based on antimicrobial and immunomodulatory mechanisms [5].

These findings concern experimental models. Reviews of peptides in sport describe KPV alongside other fragments promoted for recovery and anti-inflammatory effects, and state that most published studies examine controlled therapeutic regimens rather than the combined protocols used in bodybuilding [2]. No source reviewed reports a clinical benefit of KPV for appearance, joint recovery or skin.
No studies found. Research on KPV is limited to cell cultures and animal models, mainly colitis, along with materials-science work on delivery systems [10][11][12][15].

No human safety data for KPV were identified. A 2026 review of peptides in sport and bodybuilding lists cardiovascular strain, insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia and psychiatric instability among emerging risks of peptide use in general and notes that an unregulated supply chain increases risks because products are often mislabelled or contaminated [2]. These statements describe the class of products, not specific findings about KPV.
Grokipedia states that animal work found no pigmentation effect because KPV lacks the relevant motif of alpha-MSH [7][4].

Alpha-MSH was characterised as a neuroimmunomodulatory peptide whose anti-inflammatory influence involves inhibition of NF-kappa B, a body of work reviewed in 2000 [1][3]. Grokipedia attributes the first demonstration of the anti-inflammatory activity of the C-terminal fragment to a 1989 study by Hiltz and Lipton, with further work by Catania and Lipton in the 1990s [7]; this account has not been verified against primary sources here. A 2000 paper reported antimicrobial effects of alpha-MSH and KPV [9], a 2004 study examined alpha-MSH and KPV signalling in human keratinocytes [16], and in 2008 two papers reported PepT1-mediated uptake and efficacy in mouse colitis [8][15].

From the 2010s delivery research expanded with nanoparticle and hydrogel formulations [10][11][12]. Grokipedia reports that on 30 October 2026 the US Department of Health and Human Services published an enforcement discretion policy for 503A compounding that lists KPV along with BPC-157, epitalon, MOTS-c, semax and TB-500; the notice states that compounded drugs are not FDA-approved [7].

KPV circulates mainly through research-peptide vendors and forum discussion. On T Nation, one longtime poster describes ordering a combined bundle and calls the first three components key for soft tissue and inflammation [13]; another says they use it daily and compares outcomes for torn ligaments and sports injuries [14]. A poster in a testosterone thread mentions waiting for oral BPC and KPV [17]. Another thread asks whether KPV could be added to a TB-500 and BPC stack [18]. The forum material consists of anecdotes and recommendations and contains no controlled data.

timeline.event: Anti-inflammatory activity of the C-terminal alpha-MSH fragment KPV is reported (per Grokipedia). [7]
Reviews describe alpha-MSH and KPV effects on inflammation and host defence; antimicrobial activity reported. [1][9]
KPV is reported to reduce intestinal inflammation via PepT1 uptake and in mouse colitis models. [8][15]
Nanoparticle delivery of KPV to the colon reduces colitis in mice. [10]
Oral hyaluronic acid-functionalised nanoparticles carrying KPV tested in mouse ulcerative colitis. [11]
Reviews group KPV with peptides marketed for recovery and bodybuilding. [2]

lore.intro: KPV appears on T Nation mainly as a component of multi-peptide bundles for soft-tissue and inflammation complaints. [13][14]

claims.claim: KPV reduces inflammation and aids recovery from soft-tissue injuries.
claims.believers: Posters call KPV, BPC-157 and TB-500 'key for soft tissue and inflammation' and say they use the bundle daily after injuries [13][14].
claims.experts: Animal and cell studies show anti-inflammatory effects of KPV, mainly in colitis models; no human trials for injury recovery were identified, and reviews describe clinical evidence for peptides in sport as limited [2][6][15].

claims.claim: KPV is a gut-healing peptide that helps with bowel inflammation.
claims.believers: Users plan to order oral KPV and BPC for gut-related issues [17].
claims.experts: KPV reduced colitis in several mouse models, including with PepT1 uptake and nanoparticle delivery, but human trials have not been reported, and unformulated KPV is reported to degrade in acidic conditions [8][11][7].

claims.claim: KPV gives the benefits of alpha-MSH without pigmentation or other hormone effects.
claims.believers: Community descriptions of KPV present it as an anti-inflammatory piece of alpha-MSH.
claims.experts: A review notes that KPV lacks the sequence motif needed for melanocortin-receptor pigmentation effects, which is why it was studied as an alternative to alpha-MSH [4]; long-term effects in humans are unstudied.

claims.claim: Adding KPV to a BPC-157 and TB-500 stack is synergistic.
claims.believers: Posters ask about or recommend adding KPV to the TB-500 and BPC stack [18][13].
claims.experts: No controlled study of the combination was identified in the sources reviewed.
